item.title: Selection and shared host measurements
item.description:
These records cover exact selections and shared host setup. The controlled comparison identifies its M4 environment and revisions; the earlier single-run sample has incomplete metadata and is retained only as historical evidence. “Refactor” and “current” below identify the candidate in that comparison.

Early selection sample

The following sample was recorded in documentation commit 1f44b03. Its exact measured implementation revision, compiler build, OS version, and accelerator model were not recorded. Its driver/workload are identified, but the sample cannot support a reproducible cross-version comparison.

The focused entity_selection_benchmark.mojo workload compares ordinary full-world host execution with contiguous and disjoint 64-row selections in a 100,000-row world, a selected add/remove chain, and selected device execution when an accelerator is available. On the Apple Metal development host used for the 1.0.0b2 work, one bounded run measured approximately 0.0253 ms for the 100k-row host path, 0.0000664 ms for the contiguous selection, 0.000556 ms for 64 disjoint single-row ranges, 0.00727 ms for the add/remove chain, and 0.379 ms for the device selection. These are development measurements, not a cross-version historical baseline; use the benchmark on target hardware for regression decisions.

The manual host thread dispatch experiment compares complete sequential kernel calls with dynamically claimed whole-store and contiguous chunk jobs at 1/2/4 worker tasks, including small and large increment/compute workloads and single-store cases. Its driver, timing boundaries, reproduction commands, and Linux measurements are recorded there. It is a restricted feasibility benchmark; the current experimental engine adds eligibility and lifecycle checks absent from that prototype. Both drivers remain outside the normal PR performance gate.

Shared host execution comparison

The focused selection driver also measures thin and lexical host kernels over seven matching archetypes (512 rows each) alongside six nonmatching archetypes (512 rows each). All matching rows perform the same increment; the closure also counts range invocations. Construction and result checks are excluded, and checks outside the timer verify row count, every row against Bencher.num_iters, and the closure’s exact invocation count and accumulated values. These cases remain manual benchmarks; they are not added to the small PR suite.

On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the shared host setup refactor in 1cd32ba was compared with 688fb670c87ced6b08c920e2c3527a1890218c6f using the same updated driver and compiler environment. Build one optimized binary against an isolated baseline checkout and one against the current source, without -g, sanitizers, or tracing. Warm each once, then alternate baseline/current order across five paired samples with no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs. The driver uses fixed iterations: 100 full-world calls, 1,000 multi-archetype calls, 10,000 contiguous selected calls, and 1,000 disjoint selected calls.

Host workload Baseline median Refactor median
100,000 rows, full-world thin 23.33 µs 22.89 µs
3,584 rows, seven matching archetypes, thin 1.269 µs 1.034 µs
Same rows, lexical closure 1.089 µs 0.885 µs
64 selected contiguous rows in a 100k world 69.0 ns 18.5 ns
64 selected disjoint single-row ranges in a 100k world 690 ns 257 ns

The unchanged mutation controls measured 10.13 → 10.09 µs for a 64-row add/remove chain and 107 → 98 µs for the first 512-row disjoint mutation pass. The existing selected device case ran on the actual Apple M4 accelerator and measured 276.31 → 267.52 µs. These short synthetic batches are local evidence, not portable timing baselines or application speedup claims. Full-world row work dominates discovery at 100k rows; small selections benefit from avoiding matching-range allocation. Compilation is excluded from every operation timing. The initial baseline driver build took 18.65 seconds; a repeated current build took 1.36 seconds with local compiler caches populated. These build times are not comparable cold-compilation measurements and establish no compilation speedup. Linux operation timings remain unmeasured locally.

Reproduce with the current driver against both libraries:

pixi run mojo build -I /path/to/baseline/src benchmark/entity_selection_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-selection-base
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/entity_selection_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-selection-current
/tmp/larecs-selection-base
/tmp/larecs-selection-current

Storage range migration

The #170 comparison uses the current selection and migration drivers against PR212, including the 100k-row ordinary host path and 65,536-row whole-archetype batches. Concurrent sibling builds overlapped every sample, so these results support no controlled regression or speedup claim. Query/range metadata sharing is checked directly in the cursor regression tests.

item.title: Threaded host measurements
item.description:
The measurements below concern the implemented engine at 4489ceb, on AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux x86-64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), MAX 26.5.0. The host-dispatch feasibility investigation retains a different prototype and must not substitute for this engine.

Threaded host execution

benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo measures the implemented public SystemContext.run[kernel, threaded=True]() against unchanged sequential calls. Both worlds have identical initial rows, arithmetic, and layout. The driver covers 1/2/4 worker tasks, one/four stores, balanced and seven-to-one skewed stores, 1,024–1,048,576 total rows, and increments or 32 dependent arithmetic rounds per row. It forces min_parallel_rows=0 to expose dispatch overhead; configured one-worker runs still use whole-range sequential fallback.

Each case warms both paths twice, calibrates the sequential path to a 10 ms batch or at most 4,096 calls, then alternates order across five paired samples. Complete-call timing includes discovery, validation, spatial-invalidation checks, resource binding, context allocation, atomic claiming, dispatch, join, cleanup, and world-size consumption. Construction, initial runtime warmup, compilation, and exact result validation are excluded. Every final row is validated against all warmup, calibration, and measured calls. No resources or spatial classifiers are bound; shared-resource, selected, and partitioned correctness lives in the tests, while their performance remains unmeasured here.

pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark
/tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark
/tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark
/tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark

Build once without debug info, tracing, or sanitizers. Run measurements without other builds or benchmark jobs. Each PAIR line contains skew flag, base rows per store, store count, arithmetic rounds, worker count, pair index, calls per batch, sequential ns/call, and threaded ns/call. In skewed cases, total rows are ten times the base row count. Report compilation separately and retain hardware/compiler details; this synthetic comparison establishes no portable cutoff, fixed speedup, or application-level benefit.

At revision 4489ceb, on Linux x86-64 (7.2.5-3-omarchy), AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U (8 cores, 16 hardware threads), Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), and MAX 26.5.0, the optimized build took 17.57 seconds in the installed environment; this is not a cold-cache compilation measurement. Three serial binary runs took 7.12, 7.48, and 7.70 seconds after regression builds completed. All 30 scenarios and 450 paired measurements passed exact result validation. Raw local output is retained in ignored output/threaded-execution/run-{1,2,3}.txt files.

Four-worker results below summarize 15 pairs per case. Times are medians in microseconds per complete call; speedup is the median paired ratio, so it need not equal the ratio of the displayed medians.

Total rows Stores Work per row Sequential µs Threaded µs Speedup
1,024 4 balanced increment 0.718 16.072 0.04×
65,536 4 balanced 32 rounds 1,869.585 550.040 3.44×
262,144 1 increment 100.969 46.486 2.24×
1,048,576 4 balanced increment 406.295 141.176 2.95×
1,048,576 1 32 rounds 32,106.429 8,967.991 3.50×
163,840 4 skewed 32 rounds 4,999.816 1,455.091 3.39×

This is one developer machine with unpinned affinity and frequency. Tiny increments lose substantially when the row cutoff is explicitly disabled; the default cutoff avoids that dispatch. These measurements cover neither macOS arm64 nor application kernels, shared-resource workloads, exact selections, spatial maintenance, or partitioned layouts. The engine remains experimental.

item.title: Synchronization measurement protocol
item.description:
This record preserves the standalone driver protocol. No hardware, compiler, run revision, or timing results were recorded with this section, so it makes no measured performance claim. The driver is available at the documentation revision through its source. Current implementation details are in synchronization internals.

Synchronization primitives

benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo is a focused manual comparison of 100,000 sequential scalar increments using a plain scalar control, direct Mojo relaxed atomics, Larecs relaxed atomic views, and uncontended write guards. Every case performs equivalent increments and consumes results. Setup and final exact total validation are excluded; guard acquisition, payload access, and release are included. These are isolated uncontended costs, not complete ECS execution, contention, allocation, transfer, or GPU measurements. No new timing cases are added to the normal PR performance suite.

Build once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing, warm the binary, then run repeated samples without other builds or benchmark jobs:

pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-synchronization
/tmp/larecs-synchronization

Report compilation time separately from execution and retain hardware/compiler details with timing claims. Concurrent compound access and exact atomic totals are correctness checks in test/synchronization_test.mojo; contended performance and complete binding/transfer measurements remain roadmap work.

item.title: Deferred classification measurements
item.description:
This report retains M4 results for implementation 76868ef based on 0241e91, with Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567). The original run did not record an OS build. The current maintenance mechanism can differ from this measured revision; the workloads and timing exclusions follow below. “Current” below refers to the measured implementation.

Deferred dirty classification

Build pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/dirty_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-dirty-spatial, then run that binary with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. It constructs identical scrambled 2,048/32,768-entity worlds with 72 component bytes per row plus entity IDs, establishes initial spatial order, warms both paths, and alternates five paired samples of sixteen frames (1,024 frames for clean boundaries to resolve their small cost). The 24 scenarios cover uniform (16 entities/cell), dense (256/cell), and sparse (16/cell with key gaps of 128) distributions, with 0, 1, 1/64, or all identities updated. Each updated identity receives two reference writes per frame; classification observes final values. On alternating frames those writes cancel. Other frames advance cells by one. Both paths perform identical updates and semantic work.

The deferred path uses automatic tracking. Its control requests a full rebuild after those same writes. Timings include updates, marking, key scratch allocation, classification, sorting, typed movement of all columns, and location repair. Construction, registration, initial maintenance, and correctness checks are excluded. Every sample validates complete key order, each identity/location, the expected final input for every identity, and all eight payload lanes outside timing through read-only queries. Output records rows, distribution, dirty count, pair number, and deferred/full frame ns. This compares current deferred maintenance with current explicit full rebuilds; it does not measure a historical implementation or total application speedup.

Clean calls do no row work. Dirty calls still copy O(entity-ID capacity) keys and inspect affected archetypes, so sparse classification is not O(D) complete maintenance. Full rebuilds currently reset sparse membership and caches. Dense updates may favor contiguous full classification; structural-heavy workloads use full rebuilds. Retained keys/membership cost at least nine bytes per allocated ID plus queue capacity (full ID/generation identities and allocator slack). Scratch and movement metadata add temporary memory. These are layout costs, not measured application memory usage.

A local run on Apple M4, arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567) with implementation 76868ef (based on 0241e91) built the optimized driver in 4.74 seconds. Five warmed pairs gave these median complete-frame times for 32,768 entities:

Distribution Dirty identities Deferred Explicit full rebuild Deferred/full
Uniform 1 0.685 ms 1.076 ms 0.637
Uniform 512 0.749 ms 1.133 ms 0.661
Dense 512 0.811 ms 1.194 ms 0.679
Sparse 1 0.097 ms 0.490 ms 0.198
Sparse 512 0.112 ms 0.497 ms 0.226
Uniform 32,768 0.850 ms 0.858 ms 0.991

Across both sizes and all distributions, nonzero sparse-update scenarios took 19.5–67.9% of the full-rebuild frame time. Clean boundaries measured approximately 3–4 ns (close to timer resolution), versus 0.031/0.490 ms full rebuilds at the two sizes. Fully dirty frames took 99.1–104.6% of the explicit control. An earlier version that resolved every dirty identity separately took 131–141% for fully dirty frames; the accepted all-ID-dirty fallback avoids that column/location setup cost. Neither path can avoid moving clean rows when regrouping demands it.

The separate same-driver PR gate against 0241e91 passed all 12 core and 32 spatial cases in 41.1 seconds including four sequential compilations and five paired samples. It found no confirmed regression under the existing 30%/500 ns rule. It still measured approximately 15–19% overhead for reversing maintenance, 10–14% for maintained mobile frames, and 3–8% for ordinary stable-ID access. Those costs remain visible tradeoffs, not claims of zero regression. Linux evidence comes from the PR checks; actual GPU execution is validated separately and is not included in these CPU performance numbers.

item.title: Partition layout measurements
item.description:
These comparisons have distinct layouts and environments. The Linux report compares growable stores with 256-row-capped blocks; the macOS report compares historical bounded blocks with row reordering. Keep those controls separate. The growable results were recorded in documentation commit 6d7c2ea; its text does not identify an exact current implementation SHA beyond decision 0014. The macOS comparison does identify its implementation and base revisions. Below, “current” refers to the candidate in each comparison.

Partitioned storage comparison

Build the optimized standalone driver once: pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/partitioned_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-partition-benchmark. Run that binary without concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Partitioning is explicitly selected at registration; the control is the same current library’s deferred row reordering, not forced full classification or a historical library with different invalidation costs. The existing core/spatial PR gate separately measures changes to the default paths against the exact base.

The driver constructs identical deterministic scrambled 2,048/32,768-row worlds with two component-defined archetypes, 64-byte SIMD payloads, an integer input, and an additional eight-byte column on half the rows. It compares one growable store per logical cluster with row reordering for uniform (16 identities per cell), dense (1,024 per cell), and singleton sparse (one identity per cell, key spacing 128) distributions. Each configuration warms both layouts with one sixteen-frame batch, then alternates their order for five paired sixteen-frame samples.

The 48 scenarios cover maintenance with 1, 1/64, or all identities updated; ordinary read-only query scans and host execution with unchanged layouts; and complete cell frames with the same updates, maintenance every frame (or every fourth frame for 1/64 updates), all-lane per-cell aggregation, and cyclic adjacent-cell aggregate products. Both layouts use identical entities, input updates, and semantic work. The scan controls still call the clean boundary. All measured update frames include marking, pending key allocation/copy, classification, directory construction or sorting, column growth/movement, source swap-removal, location repair, and allocation reclamation as applicable. Cell frames also include query setup, cell scratch allocation, aggregation, and neighbor arithmetic. Construction, initial placement, policy/device setup, and validation are excluded. There are no device transfers in these CPU timings.

Every sample checks all identities once, final inputs, all payload lanes, entity locations, default key order or homogeneous cluster stores, and equal complete spatial checksums outside timing. Query/host scan reductions are also checked against their complete expected sums. Results are consumed inside the timer. This is a synthetic spatial workload, not a game/simulation speedup, collision detection, or a persistent neighbor index.

MEMORY records report initial maintained capacity-derived owned bytes; MEMORY_AFTER_MOVEMENT reports retained buffers after 96 fully moving frames: physical-directory slots, component/ID buffers, entity locations, key/dirty caches, queued identities, and recycled-slot capacity. Counted allocations are physical-directory plus row-column/ID allocations. Graph/pool allocations, allocator overhead, device state, classifier configuration, and all temporary maintenance/query/cell scratch are excluded; these records are not RSS or peak memory measurements. The components are trivial and have no hidden payload heap. Columns in a store share capacity, but each column and the IDs allocate separately. PAIR records give rows, distribution, mode, update count, cadence, pair index, reordering ns/frame, and partition ns/frame.

Growable-store comparison on Linux

The same current driver was built against committed base df0e6c5638beaab2bf3784a2b4784044a7c2707e (256-row-capped blocks) and the growable-store implementation from decision 0014. This local run used AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 7.2.5-3-omarchy x86_64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), normal optimized builds without tracing, sanitizers, or debug information. Cold builds ran sequentially and took 11.13 s / 11.11 s (base/current). No other builds or benchmark jobs ran during timing; background desktop services remained active. Five pairs of fresh binary invocations alternated base/current order. Each invocation used the warmup, five paired sixteen-frame samples per case, timing boundaries, and complete validation described above. Values below are medians of the five per-invocation medians, in milliseconds. All 48 cases validated in all ten invocations. Median complete driver execution including validation was 13.10 s / 11.33 s (base/current).

Driver SHA-256: 37795c49baa95f1b911d43327d413097b85a5f60f92f3137accf7abfa9a90ad9.

Distribution Timed work, 32,768 rows Capped blocks Growable stores Growable / capped
Uniform Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.416 0.256 0.61
Dense Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.111 0.072 0.65
Dense Complete frame, all moving 6.032 4.295 0.71
Singleton sparse Complete frame, all moving 20.400 17.231 0.84
Dense Ordinary query scan, clean 0.430 0.427 0.99
Dense Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.030 0.031 1.03
Uniform Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.068 0.070 1.03
Singleton sparse Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.337 0.344 1.02

Dense initial placement used 64 stores and 225 counted allocations, versus 128 blocks and 449 allocations in the base. Initial counted owned bytes fell from 4,448,265 to 4,403,209. After 96 fully moving frames, growable dense stores retained 7,847,945 bytes and 64,512 row slots, versus 5,062,665 bytes and 32,768 slots for capped blocks. Destination stores can grow while their old rows are still awaiting transfer, and nonempty stores retain that spare capacity. Fewer stores therefore do not guarantee less retained memory. These remain capacity-derived buffer measurements, with the exclusions described above.

Full scans changed by -0.8% to +4.3% across these distributions; small timing differences on this desktop runner do not establish a scan improvement. Maintenance and fully moving frame results favor growable stores here, but singleton clusters still have separate allocations and substantial traversal overhead. This is CPU-only synthetic evidence; macOS, GPU, application, peak memory, and additional component-width comparisons remain on the roadmap. Local raw reports are retained under output/performance/growable_clusters/.

Historical bounded-block comparison on macOS

The measurements below are historical evidence for decision 0013’s 256-row-capped blocks, not timings for the current growable-store layout. Dense clusters now use fewer stores; sparse clusters still require separate allocations. Rerun the driver before making performance claims about the new layout.

A local optimized run on Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), implementation f3d99cd (base 6037850), built in 7.59 seconds and completed execution/validation in 8.88 seconds. Driver SHA-256: da005387b10958c875771cdfb16cebbe455aa7e883631ef36f021734f355a787. No concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. Representative medians across five warmed pairs for 32,768 rows were:

Distribution Timed work Updates / cadence Reordering Partitions Partition / reorder
Uniform Maintenance 1 / every frame 0.626 ms 0.336 ms 0.54
Uniform Maintenance 512 / every frame 1.334 ms 0.381 ms 0.29
Dense Maintenance 1 / every frame 0.600 ms 0.017 ms 0.03
Dense Maintenance 512 / every frame 1.348 ms 0.096 ms 0.07
Uniform Complete cell frame 512 / every fourth frame 0.627 ms 0.393 ms 0.63
Dense Complete cell frame 512 / every fourth frame 0.651 ms 0.293 ms 0.45
Uniform Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.956 ms 2.785 ms 1.42
Dense Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.881 ms 3.125 ms 1.66
Singleton sparse Complete cell frame All / every frame 1.357 ms 17.011 ms 12.54
Uniform Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.175 ms 1.17
Dense Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.148 ms 0.99
Singleton sparse Ordinary query scan Clean 0.149 ms 0.237 ms 1.59
Uniform Ordinary host scan Clean 0.019 ms 0.045 ms 2.36
Dense Ordinary host scan Clean 0.019 ms 0.022 ms 1.16
Singleton sparse Ordinary host scan Clean 0.020 ms 0.155 ms 7.92

Initial maintained capacity and allocation evidence for those worlds:

Layout / distribution Counted owned bytes Counted row/directory allocations Partition blocks Row capacity / live rows
Reordering, all distributions 4,359,561 8 0 32,768 / 32,768
Partitions, uniform 7,241,737 14,337 4,096 32,768 / 32,768
Partitions, dense 4,448,265 449 128 32,768 / 32,768
Partitions, singleton sparse 27,426,825 114,689 32,768 32,768 / 32,768

All initial blocks were fully occupied at their allocated capacities. Component capacity alone therefore understates partition overhead: physical-store metadata and many separate allocations matter, especially for singleton clusters. At 2,048 rows counted bytes were 273,801 for reordering versus 452,617 uniform, 278,025 dense, and 1,714,185 singleton partition storage. After 96 fully moving frames, counted retained bytes were 4,883,849 for reordering versus 10,116,809 uniform, 5,062,665 dense, and 51,019,785 singleton partitions at 32,768 rows. Uniform partition row capacity grew to 58,320; dense/singleton row capacity remained 32,768. Empty blocks released their row allocations, while partial block growth and high-water directory/queue capacity remained. These are retained-buffer measurements, not peak memory.

Small dense/uniform updates took less elapsed maintenance time with partitions, while directory rebuilding and per-block scans dominated singleton cases. The benchmark measures total elapsed costs, not byte-movement counters. Fully moving workloads were slower despite local transfer. Keep partitions opt-in, and retain the reordering default. The measured bounded-block implementation copied identity-capacity keys, inspected blocks, and could move unchanged rows during same-cluster compaction. The current layout retains key copying and directory scans but removes cross-block compaction; destination growth can still relocate existing columns. Cluster selection scans metadata. Application workloads, other component widths, structural-heavy frames, Linux comparative timings, process/peak memory, and device timings remain on the roadmap. GPU functional integration ran on the actual local accelerator; it is separate evidence from these CPU performance measurements.

The separate default-path PR gate against 6037850 passed all twelve core and 32 spatial cases in 49.2 seconds, including four sequential builds and five paired samples. It required no regression confirmation. Ordinary 2,048-row query/host execution changes were +0.1%/-0.6%, stable-ID access was +3.9%, and selected mutation was +0.9% in that run. These small shared-machine differences are not a zero-overhead guarantee; the existing 30%/500 ns rule is unchanged. Hosted Linux/macOS evidence is retained by the PR checks.

item.title: Resource execution measurements
item.description:
This report records Apple M4/macOS 27.0.1 results with Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), base 6a3841b, and the portable-adapter work recorded in fde2cb9. The original text did not identify the exact measured current-tree SHA; fde2cb9 identifies the retained report/driver, not proof of a clean timed tree. The measured read-only adapter implementation predates later mutable-adapter and device-copy-reuse work. Its transfer costs are not current API guarantees. Below, “current” means that measured candidate rather than today’s checkout.

Resource execution

resource_execution_benchmark.mojo uses the current execution API. Compare the same workload against the base library, adapting only backend call spelling when the base predates ExecutionBackend. It measures complete calls over 512 Int32 rows with either no resources or one legacy scalar resource. resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo measures current read-only adapters over the same rows and 4,096 initial Int32 samples. Only the first sample is read; the entire source is uploaded. Each timed adapter call edits that sample, and growth cases append one sample per call. Host calls use 10,000 iterations; GPU calls use 100. One warmup invocation precedes each timer. Construction and final checks are excluded; validation, leases, component transfers, resource uploads/downloads, allocation growth, and synchronization are included when applicable. Exact outputs, row counts, source values, and final sample lengths are checked outside timing.

Copy the current driver for the baseline build:

cp benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo /tmp/resource_base.mojo

If the base accepts on_device: Bool rather than backend: ExecutionBackend, adapt only that copy before compiling it:

python - <<'PYCODE'
from pathlib import Path
import re

path = Path("/tmp/resource_base.mojo")
source = path.read_text().replace("    ExecutionBackend,\n", "")
source, count = re.subn(
    r"backend=\(\s*ExecutionBackend\.DEVICE if device else ExecutionBackend\.HOST\s*\)",
    "on_device=device",
    source,
)
assert count == 4, "Review the driver before adapting a changed call matrix"
assert "ExecutionBackend" not in source.split('from std.time', 1)[1]
path.write_text(source)
PYCODE

This maps the same compile-time device boolean to the older keyword; kernels, row counts, iterations, warmup, validation, and timing boundaries stay identical. Do not substitute a historical driver with different workloads. Device comparisons require a working accelerator on both sides; an older host fallback is not a device measurement. For a base using on_gpu, use that keyword instead.

Build optimized binaries once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing:

pixi run mojo build -I /path/to/base/src /tmp/resource_base.mojo -o /tmp/resource-base
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-current
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-adapters

On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), compare base 6a3841b against this implementation with the same driver. Warm each binary, then run five paired samples, alternating base/current order, with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Median per-call means were:

Complete invocation Base Current
Host, no resource 294.2 ns 299.6 ns
Host, legacy scalar resource 299.8 ns 350.7 ns
GPU, no resource 250.50 µs 251.52 µs
GPU, legacy scalar resource 243.51 µs 268.59 µs
Host, edited adapter — 449.1 ns
Host, edited adapter plus growth — 451.4 ns
GPU, edited adapter — 323.76 µs
GPU, edited adapter plus growth — 303.54 µs

The scalar GPU case costs about 10.3% more with staged publication and lifetime protection. These measurements establish the cost of this synthetic workload, not an application speedup or Tree-D shading result. Short GPU batches are noisy; the growth-case ordering does not establish a growth benefit. Source/sample allocation and scientific preprocessing during initial construction are excluded; incremental host append and device allocation growth are included in growth cases. Existing allocation capacity is reused in nongrowing cases; contents are uploaded every run.

Sequential base/current/adapter driver builds took 1.18/3.00/3.01 seconds with existing compiler caches and no competing builds. These are recorded build costs, not comparable cold-compilation measurements. Linux resource timings and cold compilation remain unmeasured. These focused manual cases do not enlarge the normal PR performance matrix.

item.title: AoS plotting workflow evidence
item.description:
This is a dynamically regenerated comparison, not one fixed historical run. The workflow records its checkout SHA and resolves Mojo through benchmark/plots/pixi.lock; its ubuntu-24.04 label does not identify a CPU or cache size. No numerical speedup is asserted without a selected run’s data. The driver defines iteration calibration and measured work; compiler generation, world construction, plotting, and dependency setup are outside per-entity loop timing. Hosted load, changing runner hardware, and artifact retention limit cross-run interpretation.

Versus Array of Structs

The publishing-run plots show iteration time per entity for a workload that adds velocity to position in both dimensions. Historical driver fields are not the tutorial’s API: the checked particle example uses Position.x/y and Velocity.dx/dy. See the plotting driver for its exact data types.

The benchmark is performed with different amounts of “payload components”, where each of them has two Float64 fields, just like Position and Velocity. Further, the total number of entities is varied from 100 to 1 million.

Plots and raw data are available in the aos-benchmark artifact of the publishing run that produced them. Select the run for the measured checkout SHA; the report contains no fixed checked-in plot or golden timings.

The documentation workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) regenerates this plot for each published commit on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runner, using the Mojo version pinned in benchmark/plots/pixi.lock. The workflow does not record the runner’s CPU or cache sizes, and the hardware behind that runner label can change between runs. Read the plot as a comparison on one machine, not as a prediction for other hardware. Each run keeps the raw results as its aos-benchmark artifact. To measure your own machine, run pixi run plots in benchmark/plots.

item.title: Regression-check runtime evidence
item.description:
These are recorded execution budgets for an unchanged-library comparison, not platform speed rankings. The hosted record identifies merge checkout ba8b180; the earlier local record identifies baseline 688fb67 but not its exact current checkout SHA. Hardware/compiler, method, excluded costs, and confirmation limits are preserved below. Current commands and failure rules live in regression operation.

Initial gate measurements

The initial unchanged-library comparison against 688fb67 on Apple M4, macOS 27 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), took 55.3 seconds: core builds 9.3/9.6 seconds and sampling 2.6 seconds; spatial builds 5.8/5.4 seconds and sampling 22.2 seconds. Builds and samples ran sequentially; no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. These are driver compilation costs in an already installed environment, not dependency installation time.

The first hosted run compared the same unchanged library against 688fb67, using PR merge checkout ba8b180, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the same current driver on each side, fresh output binaries, sequential compilation/sampling, and five alternating pairs. Both suites passed without confirmation, and both artifact uploads succeeded:
